NeuroBridge-S4: Proxy-Data Demonstration for Small-N Human Adaptation Management¶

NeuroBridge-S4: A Small-N Human Adaptation Management Framework for Artemis II Proxy Data

NASA Artemis II - Human Research Data Methodology Challenge

NeuroBridge-S4 is a methodology for converting sparse, high-dimensional, multimodal human spaceflight-like data into individualized adaptation management profiles. It is designed for the Artemis II small-N challenge: n = 4, multimodal measures, limited sampling, no conventional statistical power, and high value of each individual trajectory.

Central message. NeuroBridge-S4 turns rare human spaceflight-like data from "too small for conventional population statistics" into "deep enough for individualized biological interpretation and adaptation management."

Reviewer Quick Start¶

Please read this first. This notebook is written to be read like a report, top to bottom.

  • This notebook demonstrates NeuroBridge-S4 using real public NHANES proxy data.
  • It does not use actual Artemis II astronaut data.
  • It does not use synthetic subjects.
  • Four real NHANES participants are selected as a real n = 4 pseudo-crew.
  • The notebook has been executed with outputs embedded, so figures and tables are already visible.
  • Reviewers can read it like a report from top to bottom.
  • Running the notebook is optional for review. Reproducibility instructions are provided (see README).

How to review this notebook in 10 minutes¶

  1. Read Reviewer Quick Start and Plain-language Project Summary.
  2. Inspect the Control Ladder and the Outputs Index.
  3. Review the reference deviation heatmap and the biological domain heatmap.
  4. Review BACI and the BACI sensitivity analysis.
  5. Compare the three graph types: conceptual knowledge graph, observed proxy graph, and decision-support graph.
  6. Read the Individual Adaptation Profiles and the Crew-Level Summary.
  7. Use the README only if computational reproduction is desired.

Plain-language Project Summary¶

NeuroBridge-S4 helps convert rare, small-sample human spaceflight-like data into interpretable adaptation profiles. Instead of asking whether four people can prove a population-level effect, the method asks what can be learned from each individual's biological pattern when it is compared with a real reference population and interpreted through connected biological systems.

What the method is for:

  • to understand which biological systems may be under strain;
  • to distinguish isolated biomarker changes from coordinated multi-system patterns;
  • to help prioritize what HRP may want to monitor next.

What the method is not for:

  • it is not intended to diagnose, and
  • it is not intended to prescribe treatment.

Everything below builds toward a short, human-readable profile for each crew member and a crew-level summary that a human-research team could act on.

What HRP Gets from This Method¶

NeuroBridge-S4 produces a structured, reusable set of decision-support outputs:

  • Individual Adaptation Profiles - one per crew member.
  • Cross-System Biological Coherence Maps - which systems move together.
  • Crew-Level Adaptation Summary - the crew at a glance, without averaging away individuals.
  • Recovery and Follow-Up Data Priorities - what to measure next.
  • Monitoring Priority Matrix - which systems deserve closer attention.
  • Countermeasure Consideration Map - which support categories are relevant.
  • A reusable analytic workflow for Standard Measures, ARCHeR, and Immune Biomarkers.

In operational terms, the method helps HRP ask and answer:

  1. What changed?
  2. In which system?
  3. Is the signal isolated or coherent across systems?
  4. Is recovery progressing?
  5. What should be monitored next?
  6. Which countermeasure category should be considered?

Interpretation Guardrails¶

Please keep these in mind while reviewing every figure and table.

  • NHANES is used as a real terrestrial proxy reference dataset, not as a substitute for Artemis II.
  • NHANES is not true astronaut data; it is a health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation.
  • The n = 4 pseudo-crew are real participants, not synthetic subjects.
  • BACI is a transparent signal-triage metric, not a validated diagnostic score.
  • Graphs are separated by type: conceptual knowledge graph, data-derived observed proxy graph, and decision-support graph - they must not be confused with one another.
  • The notebook does not diagnose medical or psychiatric conditions.
  • The notebook does not prescribe treatment.
  • The correct interpretation of every output is: "What systems should HRP look at more closely?"

Why Graph Representation Matters¶

Human adaptation is relational: sleep affects autonomic regulation, stress biology affects immune signaling, fatigue affects cognitive load. A flat table of biomarkers loses these connections. NeuroBridge-S4 therefore represents biomarkers, sleep, immune signals, cognitive load, and psychological indicators as connected biological and functional systems.

Tables break a human system into columns; graph representation helps assemble those columns back into a biological and operational system.

NeuroBridge-S4 uses three clearly distinct graph types, and they must not be confused:

  1. Biological Knowledge Graph (Section 12) - a conceptual / literature-plausible structure of how systems relate. It is not computed from NHANES and is not causal proof.
  2. Observed Proxy Coherence Graph (Section 13) - data-derived relationships computed from the real proxy reference space. It shows co-variation, not causation.
  3. Decision / Management Graph (Section 14) - a translation from biological pattern to monitoring priority and countermeasure consideration. It is an operational decision-support layer, not treatment guidance.

2. Why this notebook exists¶

Artemis II carries a very small crew. Conventional population-level statistics are weak when only four people are measured: there is no large astronaut control group, and a four-person study cannot prove population-level effects.

NeuroBridge-S4 deliberately changes the question.

  • The purpose is not to prove population-level effects.
  • The purpose is to extract structured, biologically meaningful, operationally useful information from each individual.
  • NeuroBridge-S4 treats each crew member as a longitudinal biological system, not as one data point in a group.
  • Proxy datasets act as a reference coordinate system - a way to ask "how unusual is this value?" - not as a replacement for Artemis II data.

3. Conceptual framework: from data to astronaut support¶

NeuroBridge-S4 organizes evidence into four connected levels. Lower levels are physical signals; higher levels are interpretations that those signals support.

Level 1 - Physiological and behavioral signals: sleep, activity, heart rate / heart-rate variability (HRV) where available, temperature, cardiovascular measures.

Level 2 - Biochemical and immune processes: stress hormones, inflammatory markers, immune shifts, metabolic regulation.

Level 3 - Neurobiological and cognitive functional states: autonomic regulation, circadian stability, arousal, recovery capacity, cognitive load.

Level 4 - Evidence-based psychological and operational interpretation: fatigue, workload tolerance, emotional regulation, stress perception, social/behavioral strain, recovery behavior.

The framework does not treat psychological states as isolated labels. It treats acute cognitive and psychological states as emergent functional patterns supported by converging biological, behavioral, and validated self-report evidence. A psychological interpretation is only considered when several independent measurements point the same way.

4. The Control Ladder¶

A single reference population is not enough, because astronauts are not an average sample of the public. NeuroBridge-S4 uses a Control Ladder: each reference source contributes at the level where it is scientifically strongest.

Level Reference source Role
L1 General healthy population reference Broad biological variability
L2 Health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation Closer comparison group
L3 Longitudinal wearable / sleep / stress proxy data Time-resolved physiology
L4 Spaceflight analog / bedrest data Spaceflight-like constraints
L5 Individual astronaut or pseudo-crew baseline The person's own normal

In this notebook we implement Levels 1 and 2 using NHANES. Levels 3-5 (wearables, analog/bedrest, and each astronaut's personal pre-flight baseline) would be added for full Artemis II work, using the same machinery. The figure below is generated by the code cell that follows.

# --- Shared helper functions used throughout the notebook ---------------

def save_figure(fig, name):
    # Save a figure into results/figures/ and log the path.
    path = FIGURES / name
    fig.savefig(path, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    print(f"  [saved figure] {path}")
    return path


def annotated_heatmap(ax, matrix, row_labels, col_labels, cmap="coolwarm",
                      vmin=None, vmax=None, fmt="{:.2f}", cbar_label=""):
    # A self-contained heatmap (matplotlib only) with numeric annotations.
    data = np.array(matrix, dtype=float)
    im = ax.imshow(data, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(col_labels)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(col_labels, rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(row_labels)))
    ax.set_yticklabels(row_labels)
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        for j in range(data.shape[1]):
            v = data[i, j]
            if not np.isnan(v):
                ax.text(j, i, fmt.format(v), ha="center", va="center",
                        color="black", fontsize=9)
    cb = ax.figure.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
    cb.set_label(cbar_label)
    return im

print("Helper functions defined: save_figure(), annotated_heatmap().")

Helper functions defined: save_figure(), annotated_heatmap().

5. Load real NHANES public data¶

We now download real public data from the U.S. CDC's National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), cycle 2017-2018. NHANES is a large program that combines interviews, physical examinations, and laboratory tests on thousands of participants.

Why NHANES is an appropriate proxy for this demonstration:

  • it is a population-scale terrestrial reference space;
  • it provides demographic, examination, and laboratory data in one linkable system;
  • it lets us build a health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation (a closer comparison group than the raw public sample);
  • it supports biomarker-based deviation analysis across many biological systems.

NHANES is not astronaut data and is not a substitute for Artemis II. It is one lower rung of the Control Ladder. The loader is robust: each file is downloaded independently, validated as a real SAS transport (.xpt) file by its magic bytes, and cached locally; if any file is unavailable the notebook prints a friendly warning and continues.

Technical cell: robust downloader and loader (validates SAS XPT magic bytes; caches files). Reviewers can skip; the load results are summarized in the table below.

In [5]:
# --- Robust NHANES downloader --------------------------------------------
XPT_MAGIC = b"HEADER RECORD*"  # every valid SAS transport file starts with this


def candidate_urls(fname):
    # CDC has used more than one URL layout over time; try the known-good ones in order.
    return [
        f"https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/{NHANES_YEAR}/DataFiles/{fname}",
        f"https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/{NHANES_YEAR}/DataFiles/{fname.upper()}",
        f"https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Nhanes/{NHANES_CYCLE}/{fname.upper()}",
    ]


def _download_bytes(url):
    # Prefer 'requests' (it ships trusted CA certificates via certifi); fall back to urllib.
    try:
        import requests
        resp = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "NeuroBridge-S4/1.0"}, timeout=120)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.content
    except ImportError:
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "NeuroBridge-S4/1.0"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as resp:
            return resp.read()


def fetch_xpt(fname):
    # Return a DataFrame for one NHANES file, using a local cache when possible.
    cache_path = CACHE / fname
    if cache_path.exists() and cache_path.stat().st_size > 1000:
        with open(cache_path, "rb") as fh:
            if fh.read(len(XPT_MAGIC)) == XPT_MAGIC:
                return pd.read_sas(cache_path, format="xport")

    last_error = None
    for url in candidate_urls(fname):
        try:
            data = _download_bytes(url)
            if data[:len(XPT_MAGIC)] != XPT_MAGIC:
                last_error = f"content at {url} is not a SAS transport file (likely an HTML page)"
                continue
            cache_path.write_bytes(data)
            return pd.read_sas(io.BytesIO(data), format="xport")
        except Exception as exc:
            last_error = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
            continue
    raise RuntimeError(last_error or "unknown download error")


# --- Load every file, recording success/failure --------------------------
loaded_tables = {}
load_log = []
for fname, desc in NHANES_FILES.items():
    try:
        df = fetch_xpt(fname)
        loaded_tables[fname] = df
        load_log.append({"file": fname, "description": desc, "status": "loaded",
                         "rows": df.shape[0], "columns": df.shape[1]})
        print(f"  [OK]   {fname:14s} {df.shape}  - {desc}")
    except Exception as exc:
        load_log.append({"file": fname, "description": desc, "status": "FAILED",
                         "rows": 0, "columns": 0})
        print(f"  [WARN] {fname:14s} could not be loaded: {exc}")
        print(f"         Continuing with the files that did load.")

DATA_AVAILABLE = "DEMO_J.xpt" in loaded_tables
load_log_df = pd.DataFrame(load_log)
print()
if DATA_AVAILABLE:
    print(f"Demographics loaded: real NHANES data is available. "
          f"{len(loaded_tables)}/{len(NHANES_FILES)} files loaded.")
else:
    print("STRUCTURE-ONLY FALLBACK: core demographics could not be downloaded.")
    print("No data will be fabricated. Re-run with internet access to reproduce the full demonstration.")

Technical cell: merge all files on the participant ID (SEQN) and keep examined participants.

In [7]:
# --- Merge all loaded files on the participant ID (SEQN) ------------------
if DATA_AVAILABLE:
    merged = loaded_tables["DEMO_J.xpt"][["SEQN", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "RIDSTATR"]].copy()
    for fname, df in loaded_tables.items():
        if fname == "DEMO_J.xpt":
            continue
        keep = [c for c in df.columns if c in VARIABLE_REGISTRY or c == "SEQN"]
        keep = list(dict.fromkeys(["SEQN"] + keep))  # SEQN first, de-duplicated
        merged = merged.merge(df[keep], on="SEQN", how="left")
    # Keep only participants who completed the examination (RIDSTATR == 2).
    merged = merged[merged["RIDSTATR"] == 2].drop(columns=["RIDSTATR"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    print(f"Merged dataset shape (participants x variables): {merged.shape}")
else:
    merged = pd.DataFrame(columns=["SEQN", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR"])
    print("Structure-only fallback: merged dataset is empty (no fabricated rows).")

6. Build a health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation¶

Astronauts are not equivalent to the general population, so the raw NHANES sample is not the right comparison group. We build a health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation: a healthier adult subset with lower chronic-disease burden and complete measurements. This is an approximation, not astronaut-equivalent data. We are careful not to over-filter, so a large, stable reference group remains.

Filters applied (each only if its variable is available):

  1. Adults aged 30-60 - a realistic age band.
  2. Non-smokers - excludes current smokers.
  3. Healthier metabolic/inflammatory profile - operational BMI range, non-diabetic fasting glucose, no acute inflammation.
  4. Complete core measurements - blood pressure and body measures present.
  5. Low overall missingness - at least half of the analysis biomarkers present.

Technical cell: cohort filtering. Each step records how many participants remain.

In [9]:
# --- Construct the health-filtered reference cohort, tracking each step ---
ANALYSIS_FEATURES = [f for feats in DOMAIN_FEATURES.values() for f in feats]
ANALYSIS_FEATURES = [f for f in ANALYSIS_FEATURES if f in merged.columns]

funnel = []
if DATA_AVAILABLE and len(merged) > 0:
    step = merged.copy()
    funnel.append(("All examined participants", len(step)))

    # 1. Adults aged 30-60
    step = step[step["RIDAGEYR"].between(30, 60)]
    funnel.append(("Adults aged 30-60", len(step)))

    # 2. Non-smokers (SMQ040: 1=every day, 2=some days are current smokers)
    if "SMQ040" in step.columns:
        current_smoker = step["SMQ040"].isin([1, 2])
        step = step[~current_smoker]
        funnel.append(("Non-smokers", len(step)))

    # 3. Healthier metabolic / inflammatory profile
    healthier = pd.Series(True, index=step.index)
    if "BMXBMI" in step.columns:
        healthier &= step["BMXBMI"].between(18.5, 32) | step["BMXBMI"].isna()
    if "LBXGLU" in step.columns:
        healthier &= (step["LBXGLU"] < 126) | step["LBXGLU"].isna()
    if "LBXHSCRP" in step.columns:
        healthier &= (step["LBXHSCRP"] < 10) | step["LBXHSCRP"].isna()
    step = step[healthier]
    funnel.append(("Healthier metabolic/inflammatory profile", len(step)))

    # 4. Complete core measurements: blood pressure and body measures present
    core = [c for c in ["BPXSY1", "BPXDI1", "BMXBMI"] if c in step.columns]
    if core:
        step = step.dropna(subset=core)
    funnel.append(("Complete core measurements", len(step)))

    # 5. Low overall missingness across analysis biomarkers
    if ANALYSIS_FEATURES:
        frac_present = step[ANALYSIS_FEATURES].notna().mean(axis=1)
        step = step[frac_present >= 0.5]
    funnel.append(("Health-filtered reference cohort", len(step)))

    reference_cohort = step.reset_index(drop=True)
else:
    reference_cohort = merged.copy()
    funnel.append(("Health-filtered reference cohort", len(reference_cohort)))

funnel_df = pd.DataFrame(funnel, columns=["Filtering step", "Participants remaining"])
print("Cohort filtering funnel:")
display(funnel_df)
print(f"\nHealth-filtered reference cohort size: {len(reference_cohort)} real participants.")

7. Select a real n = 4 pseudo-crew¶

The pseudo-crew is not synthetic. It is four real NHANES participants drawn from the health-filtered reference cohort. This deliberately recreates the Artemis II statistical challenge: only four people, but many measurements each. To keep the comparison honest, the four members are withheld from the reference distribution used for scoring, and are identified only by their anonymized NHANES sequence number (SEQN).

Technical cell: pseudo-crew selection (fixed random seed for reproducibility).

In [11]:
# --- Select four real participants as the pseudo-crew --------------------
PSEUDO_CREW_N = 4

if len(reference_cohort) >= PSEUDO_CREW_N:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_SEED)
    crew_idx = rng.choice(reference_cohort.index, size=PSEUDO_CREW_N, replace=False)
    pseudo_crew = reference_cohort.loc[crew_idx].reset_index(drop=True)
    # Withhold the crew from the reference distribution used for scoring.
    reference_pool = reference_cohort.drop(index=crew_idx).reset_index(drop=True)
    pseudo_crew["SEQN"] = pseudo_crew["SEQN"].astype(int)
    crew_ids = pseudo_crew["SEQN"].tolist()
    print(f"Selected {PSEUDO_CREW_N} real pseudo-crew participants (anonymized SEQN): {crew_ids}")
    print(f"Reference pool used for scoring (crew withheld): {len(reference_pool)} participants")
else:
    pseudo_crew = reference_cohort.copy()
    reference_pool = reference_cohort.copy()
    crew_ids = pseudo_crew["SEQN"].astype(int).tolist() if len(pseudo_crew) else []
    print("Structure-only fallback: not enough participants to form a pseudo-crew.")

# Compact, non-identifying feature table for the crew.
crew_display_cols = ["SEQN"] + [c for c in ["RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "BMXBMI", "BPXSY1",
                     "BPXDI1", "BPXPLS", "LBXGLU", "LBXHSCRP"] if c in pseudo_crew.columns]
print("\nPseudo-crew overview (real measurements, no personal identifiers):")
display(pseudo_crew[crew_display_cols])

8. Create reference deviation scores¶

Raw biomarkers use different units (mg/dL, mmHg, g/dL, ...), so they cannot be compared directly. NeuroBridge-S4 converts each value into a reference deviation score that answers a single plain-English question:

"How unusual is this participant's value compared with the health-filtered reference cohort?"

For each feature we compute the reference mean and standard deviation from the reference pool (crew withheld), then for each crew member: z = (the person's value - reference mean) / reference standard deviation. A z near 0 means "typical for this cohort"; a large positive or negative z means "unusual - worth a closer look." We deliberately call these reference deviations, never "abnormal" and never diagnostic.

Technical cell: reference deviation (z-score) computation.

In [13]:
# --- Compute reference deviation (z) scores for the pseudo-crew ----------
MIN_REF_N = 50  # minimum non-missing reference values required to score a feature

scored_features = []
ref_stats = {}
for feat in ANALYSIS_FEATURES:
    ref_vals = reference_pool[feat].dropna() if feat in reference_pool.columns else pd.Series(dtype=float)
    if len(ref_vals) >= MIN_REF_N and ref_vals.std(ddof=0) > 0:
        ref_stats[feat] = {"mean": ref_vals.mean(), "std": ref_vals.std(ddof=0),
                           "values": ref_vals.values}
        scored_features.append(feat)

deviation_rows = {}
percentile_rows = {}
for _, member in pseudo_crew.iterrows():
    seqn = int(member["SEQN"])
    z_scores, pcts = {}, {}
    for feat in scored_features:
        val = member[feat]
        if pd.isna(val):
            z_scores[feat], pcts[feat] = np.nan, np.nan
        else:
            s = ref_stats[feat]
            z_scores[feat] = (val - s["mean"]) / s["std"]
            pcts[feat] = float((s["values"] < val).mean() * 100.0)
    deviation_rows[f"Crew {seqn}"] = z_scores
    percentile_rows[f"Crew {seqn}"] = pcts

deviation_scores = pd.DataFrame(deviation_rows).T
percentile_scores = pd.DataFrame(percentile_rows).T
deviation_scores.columns = [VARIABLE_REGISTRY.get(c, (c,))[0] for c in deviation_scores.columns]

print(f"Scored {len(scored_features)} biomarkers with sufficient reference data.")
print("\nReference deviation (z-score) table:")
display(deviation_scores.round(2))

9. Map features into biological domains¶

A single biomarker is rarely meaningful on its own. NeuroBridge-S4 groups variables into biological domains so that reviewers can interpret systems, not scattered numbers. For each crew member we compute the mean absolute deviation within each domain - a compact measure of "how strained is this whole system?"

Technical cell: domain-level aggregation of deviation scores.

In [15]:
# --- Compute mean absolute deviation per biological domain ---------------
present_domains = {}
for domain, feats in DOMAIN_FEATURES.items():
    feats_present = [f for f in feats if f in scored_features]
    if feats_present:
        present_domains[domain] = feats_present

domain_rows = {}
for member_label in deviation_scores.index:
    # work from the un-relabeled z-scores so we can index by NHANES code
    seqn = int(member_label.split()[1])
    member = pseudo_crew[pseudo_crew["SEQN"] == seqn].iloc[0]
    row = {}
    for domain, feats in present_domains.items():
        zs = []
        for f in feats:
            val = member[f]
            if not pd.isna(val):
                s = ref_stats[f]
                zs.append(abs((val - s["mean"]) / s["std"]))
        row[domain] = float(np.mean(zs)) if zs else np.nan
    domain_rows[member_label] = row

domain_scores = pd.DataFrame(domain_rows).T
print("Mean absolute reference deviation by biological domain:")
display(domain_scores.round(2))

10. BACI: the Biological Adaptation Coherence Index¶

BACI = Biological Adaptation Coherence Index. It is a transparent signal-triage metric, not a diagnosis and not a validated clinical score. It asks one operationally useful question:

"Are multiple biological domains shifting together strongly enough to justify closer review?"

The logic is conservative: an isolated biomarker change is weak evidence, while a coordinated, multi-domain shift is more meaningful. BACI is computed transparently from quantities you can see in the tables above and normalized to 0-100. It reflects:

  • breadth - the number of shifted domains (mean |z| above a threshold);
  • magnitude - how large those shifts are;
  • spread - whether shifts span several independent biological systems;
  • (and, in future longitudinal Artemis II use, temporal alignment and recovery delay).
BACI Category
0-25 low coherence
25-50 mild coherence
50-75 moderate coherence
75-100 high coherence

Technical cell: BACI is defined as a small, readable function so it can be re-run at several thresholds (Section 11).

In [17]:
# --- Compute BACI for each pseudo-crew member ----------------------------
SHIFT_THRESHOLD = 1.0  # a domain is 'shifted' when mean |z| exceeds this


def classify_baci(score):
    if score < 25:
        return "low coherence"
    if score < 50:
        return "mild coherence"
    if score < 75:
        return "moderate coherence"
    return "high coherence"


def compute_baci(threshold):
    # Transparent signal-triage score in 0-100, combining breadth, magnitude, and spread.
    rows = []
    n_dom = domain_scores.shape[1] if not domain_scores.empty else 0
    for member_label, row in domain_scores.iterrows():
        vals = row.dropna()
        if len(vals) == 0 or n_dom == 0:
            rows.append({"crew": member_label, "BACI": 0.0, "category": "low coherence",
                         "shifted_domains": 0})
            continue
        shifted = vals[vals >= threshold]
        breadth = len(shifted) / n_dom
        magnitude = float(np.clip((shifted.mean() if len(shifted) else vals.mean()) / 3.0, 0, 1))
        spread = float(np.clip((len(shifted) - 1) / max(n_dom - 1, 1), 0, 1)) if len(shifted) else 0.0
        raw = 0.40 * breadth + 0.35 * magnitude + 0.25 * spread
        score = round(100.0 * raw, 1)
        rows.append({"crew": member_label, "BACI": score, "category": classify_baci(score),
                     "shifted_domains": int(len(shifted))})
    if not rows:
        out = pd.DataFrame(columns=["BACI", "category", "shifted_domains"])
        out.index.name = "crew"
        return out
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("crew")


baci_scores = compute_baci(SHIFT_THRESHOLD)
print(f"Biological Adaptation Coherence Index (BACI) at threshold {SHIFT_THRESHOLD}:")
display(baci_scores)

Reviewer note:

  • What it shows: how coherent each member's multi-system signal is, on a 0-100 triage scale.
  • Why it matters for HRP: it separates "one odd number" from "several systems moving together," which deserves closer review.
  • Takeaway: BACI is a prioritization aid, not a diagnosis; higher scores simply mean "look here first."

11. BACI sensitivity analysis¶

A triage metric is only trustworthy if it is not fragile. Here we recompute BACI at three "shift" thresholds - 0.75, 1.00, and 1.25 - and check whether the ranking of crew members stays stable.

  • If the ranking is stable, this supports the robustness of the signal-triage logic.
  • If the ranking changes, this reveals threshold sensitivity that HRP experts should review.

Technical cell: recompute BACI across thresholds and assess ranking stability.

In [19]:
# --- BACI sensitivity across thresholds ----------------------------------
THRESHOLDS = [0.75, 1.00, 1.25]
sens_rows = []
rankings = {}
for t in THRESHOLDS:
    b = compute_baci(t)
    rankings[t] = list(b["BACI"].sort_values(ascending=False).index)
    for crew_label, r in b.iterrows():
        sens_rows.append({"participant": crew_label, "threshold": t,
                          "BACI": r["BACI"], "category": r["category"]})

baci_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(sens_rows)
baci_sensitivity.to_csv(RESULTS / "baci_sensitivity.csv", index=False)
print("BACI across thresholds:")
display(baci_sensitivity.pivot(index="participant", columns="threshold", values="BACI"))

ranking_stable = all(rankings[THRESHOLDS[0]] == rankings[t] for t in THRESHOLDS)
print(f"\nRanking identical across all thresholds: {ranking_stable}")
if ranking_stable:
    print("  -> Interpretation: the signal-triage ranking is robust to threshold choice.")
else:
    print("  -> Interpretation: ranking shifts with threshold; HRP experts should review borderline members.")

BACI across thresholds:
threshold 0.75 1.00 1.25

Crew 94465 53.1 22.1 22.1
Crew 97774 49.1 41.5 41.5

Ranking identical across all thresholds: False

In [20]:
# --- Figure: BACI sensitivity --------------------------------------------
if not baci_sensitivity.empty:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.2))
    for crew_label in baci_sensitivity["participant"].unique():
        sub = baci_sensitivity[baci_sensitivity["participant"] == crew_label].sort_values("threshold")
        ax.plot(sub["threshold"], sub["BACI"], marker="o", linewidth=2, label=crew_label)
    for thr in (25, 50, 75):
        ax.axhline(thr, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7)
    ax.set_xticks(THRESHOLDS)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
    ax.set_xlabel("Shift threshold (domain mean |z| required to count as 'shifted')")
    ax.set_ylabel("BACI (0-100)")
    ax.set_title("Is the BACI ranking stable?\nBACI for each pseudo-crew member across shift thresholds")
    ax.legend(title="Pseudo-crew", fontsize=9)
    save_figure(fig, "baci_sensitivity_analysis.png")
    plt.show()

  • Why it matters for HRP: it demonstrates that the triage signal is examined for robustness, not presented as a single fragile number.
  • Takeaway: stable ordering across thresholds supports trusting the relative prioritization; any crossing lines flag members worth a manual second look.

12. Biological Knowledge Graph (conceptual)¶

This is graph type 1 of 3: a conceptual graph. It represents literature-plausible biological and operational relationships used for interpretation. It is not computed from NHANES and is not causal proof. It is the scientific map that connects biochemistry, neurobiology, cognitive function, evidence-based psychology, and the operational endpoints (monitoring priority and countermeasure consideration).

Technical cell: builds the conceptual knowledge graph with networkx.

In [21]:
# --- Build and draw the conceptual biological knowledge graph ------------
KNOWLEDGE_NODES = {
    "Sleep / circadian rhythm": "behavioral",

13. Observed Proxy Coherence Graph (data-derived)¶

This is graph type 2 of 3: a data-derived graph. Unlike the conceptual map above, this graph is computed from the real NHANES proxy reference space. It shows which measured biomarkers tend to move together (co-vary) in the health-filtered reference cohort. Edge thickness reflects correlation strength. This is observed co-variation, not causal proof.

Technical cell: graph construction from real correlations in the reference pool.

In [22]:
# --- Build the observed coherence graph from real correlations -----------
CORR_THRESHOLD = 0.35
corr_feats = [f for f in scored_features]
made_graph = False
if len(corr_feats) >= 3 and len(reference_pool) > MIN_REF_N:
    corr = reference_pool[corr_feats].corr()
    Gc = nx.Graph()
    for f in corr_feats:
        Gc.add_node(f, domain=VARIABLE_REGISTRY.get(f, ("", "Other"))[1])
    edge_weights = []
    for i, a in enumerate(corr_feats):
        for b in corr_feats[i + 1:]:
            r = corr.loc[a, b]
            if pd.notna(r) and abs(r) >= CORR_THRESHOLD:
                Gc.add_edge(a, b, weight=abs(r), sign=np.sign(r))
                edge_weights.append((a, b, r))

    domain_palette = {
        "Cardiovascular regulation": "#80b1d3", "Metabolic regulation": "#fdb462",
        "Body composition / physical status": "#b3de69", "Inflammation / immune-adjacent": "#fb8072",
        "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying": "#bc80bd", "Recovery-related markers": "#8dd3c7",
    }
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(15, 12))
    posc = nx.spring_layout(Gc, seed=RANDOM_SEED, k=2.6, iterations=400, scale=2.4)
    node_colors = [domain_palette.get(VARIABLE_REGISTRY.get(n, ("", "Other"))[1], "#cccccc")
                   for n in Gc.nodes()]
    for a, b, r in edge_weights:
        ax.plot([posc[a][0], posc[b][0]], [posc[a][1], posc[b][1]],
                color="#d7301f" if r > 0 else "#2166ac",
                linewidth=1 + 4 * abs(r), alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
    nx.draw_networkx_nodes(Gc, posc, ax=ax, node_color=node_colors, node_size=1200,
                           edgecolors="#333333", linewidths=1.2)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(Gc, posc, ax=ax, font_size=7,
                            labels={n: "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(VARIABLE_REGISTRY.get(n, (n,))[0], 12))
                                    for n in Gc.nodes()})
    handles = [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w", markerfacecolor=c, markersize=12, label=d)
               for d, c in domain_palette.items()]
    handles += [plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#d7301f", lw=3, label="positive correlation"),
                plt.Line2D([0], [0], color="#2166ac", lw=3, label="negative correlation")]
    ax.legend(handles=handles, fontsize=8, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1.0), framealpha=0.95)
    ax.set_title(f"Which biomarkers actually move together in the proxy data?\nObserved proxy graph: data-derived co-variation (|r| >= {CORR_THRESHOLD}); not causal proof")
    ax.axis("off")
    save_figure(fig, "observed_proxy_coherence_graph.png")
    plt.show()
    made_graph = True
    print(f"Edges drawn (|correlation| >= {CORR_THRESHOLD}): {len(edge_weights)}")
if not made_graph:
    print("Not enough scored features / reference data to build the observed coherence graph.")

  [saved figure] results/figures/observed_proxy_coherence_graph.png

Edges drawn (|correlation| >= 0.35): 12

Reviewer note:

  • What it shows: real co-variation in the proxy reference space - red links rise/fall together, blue links move oppositely; thicker = stronger.
  • Why it matters for HRP: it separates "what the literature expects" (Section 12) from "what this real dataset actually shows."
  • Takeaway: clusters tend to form along biological-domain lines, which supports grouping variables into domains - but this is co-variation, not causation.

14. Decision / Management Graph¶

This is graph type 3 of 3: a decision-support graph. It translates biological patterns into HRP-relevant monitoring priorities, follow-up data streams, and countermeasure considerations. It contains no treatment language - it answers "what should HRP look at and consider monitoring next?", not "what should be prescribed?"

Technical cell: builds the decision/management graph with networkx.

In [23]:

15. Individual Adaptation Networks¶

A crew-level average can hide what matters most: individual patterns. NeuroBridge-S4 draws an individual adaptation network for each pseudo-crew member, so each person can be understood as a distinct biological system. Node size and color reflect how strained each domain is; edges are the known biological relationships between domains. One figure is saved per participant, plus a combined panel.

Technical cell: per-member adaptation networks and a combined 2x2 panel.

In [24]:
# --- Known relationships between biological domains ----------------------
DOMAIN_EDGES = [
    ("Cardiovascular regulation", "Inflammation / immune-adjacent"),
    ("Cardiovascular regulation", "Metabolic regulation"),
    ("Metabolic regulation", "Inflammation / immune-adjacent"),
    ("Metabolic regulation", "Body composition / physical status"),
    ("Inflammation / immune-adjacent", "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying"),
    ("Inflammation / immune-adjacent", "Recovery-related markers"),
    ("Hematologic / oxygen-carrying", "Recovery-related markers"),
    ("Body composition / physical status", "Cardiovascular regulation"),
]

SHORT_DOMAIN = {
    "Cardiovascular regulation": "Cardio",
    "Metabolic regulation": "Metabolic",
    "Body composition / physical status": "Body comp.",
    "Inflammation / immune-adjacent": "Inflammation",
    "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying": "Hematologic",
    "Recovery-related markers": "Recovery",
}


def draw_individual_network(ax, member_label, domain_row):
    Gi = nx.Graph()
    domains = list(domain_scores.columns)
    for d in domains:
        Gi.add_node(d)
    for a, b in DOMAIN_EDGES:
        if a in domains and b in domains:
            Gi.add_edge(a, b)
    posi = nx.circular_layout(Gi)
    vals = np.array([domain_row.get(d, np.nan) for d in domains], dtype=float)
    vals = np.nan_to_num(vals, nan=0.0)
    sizes = 600 + 1400 * np.clip(vals / 2.5, 0, 1)
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(Gi, posi, ax=ax, edge_color="#bbbbbb", width=1.5)
    nodes = nx.draw_networkx_nodes(Gi, posi, ax=ax, node_color=vals, cmap="YlOrRd",
                                   vmin=0, vmax=2.5, node_size=sizes,
                                   edgecolors="#333333", linewidths=1.2)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(Gi, posi, ax=ax, font_size=8,
                            labels={d: SHORT_DOMAIN.get(d, d) for d in domains})
    ax.set_title(member_label, fontsize=11)
    ax.axis("off")
    return nodes


for member_label, domain_row in domain_scores.iterrows():
    seqn = int(member_label.split()[1])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6))
    nodes = draw_individual_network(ax, member_label, domain_row)
    cb = fig.colorbar(nodes, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
    cb.set_label("domain deviation (mean |z|)")
    fig.suptitle(f"Individual Adaptation Network - {member_label}", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    save_figure(fig, f"individual_adaptation_network_{seqn}.png")
    plt.close(fig)

if not domain_scores.empty:
    n_members = len(domain_scores)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 11))
    axes = axes.flatten()
    last_nodes = None
    for i, (member_label, domain_row) in enumerate(domain_scores.iterrows()):
        last_nodes = draw_individual_network(axes[i], member_label, domain_row)
    for j in range(n_members, len(axes)):
        axes[j].axis("off")
    fig.suptitle("Each pseudo-crew member as a distinct biological system\nIndividual Adaptation Networks",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    if last_nodes is not None:
        cb = fig.colorbar(last_nodes, ax=axes.tolist(), fraction=0.03, pad=0.02)
        cb.set_label("domain deviation (mean |z|)")
    save_figure(fig, "individual_adaptation_networks_panel.png")
    plt.show()

  • Why it matters for HRP: even within the same four-person group, adaptation patterns differ - some concentrated, some broad.
  • Takeaway: this is the core of NeuroBridge-S4 - individualized interpretation rather than a single crew average.

16. Countermeasure Priority Map¶

This map links detected patterns to operational support categories. It is decision-support, not medical advice: we use the language of monitoring priority, follow-up data stream, and countermeasure consideration - never treatment or diagnosis.

Technical cell: conceptual mapping of pattern -> support category, rendered as a matrix.

In [25]:
# --- Conceptual mapping: detected pattern -> management priority ---------
PATTERNS = [
    "Sleep / circadian + autonomic strain",
    "Stress / immune coherence",
    "Metabolic / fatigue pattern",
    "Cognitive-fatigue pattern",
    "Delayed recovery pattern",
    "Acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability",
]
PRIORITIES = [
    "Sleep / circadian support", "Workload pacing", "Immune follow-up", "Cognitive monitoring",
    "Psychological check-in", "Recovery protocol", "Nutrition / hydration review",
    "Additional biomarker sampling",
]
PRIORITY_MAP = {
    "Sleep / circadian + autonomic strain":
        ["Sleep / circadian support", "Workload pacing", "Cognitive monitoring", "Additional biomarker sampling"],
    "Stress / immune coherence":
        ["Immune follow-up", "Psychological check-in", "Recovery protocol", "Additional biomarker sampling"],
    "Metabolic / fatigue pattern":
        ["Nutrition / hydration review", "Workload pacing", "Additional biomarker sampling"],
    "Cognitive-fatigue pattern":
        ["Cognitive monitoring", "Workload pacing", "Sleep / circadian support", "Psychological check-in"],
    "Delayed recovery pattern":
        ["Recovery protocol", "Additional biomarker sampling", "Nutrition / hydration review"],
    "Acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability":
        ["Psychological check-in", "Cognitive monitoring", "Sleep / circadian support", "Workload pacing"],
}

priority_matrix = np.zeros((len(PATTERNS), len(PRIORITIES)))
for i, pat in enumerate(PATTERNS):
    for pr in PRIORITY_MAP[pat]:
        priority_matrix[i, PRIORITIES.index(pr)] = 1.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5.5))
annotated_heatmap(ax, priority_matrix, PATTERNS, PRIORITIES, cmap="Greens",
                  vmin=0, vmax=1, fmt="{:.0f}", cbar_label="relevant (1) / not flagged (0)")
ax.set_title("From biological pattern to operational support category\nCountermeasure Priority Map (decision-support, not treatment)")
save_figure(fig, "countermeasure_priority_map.png")
plt.show()

17. What Each NeuroBridge-S4 Layer Adds¶

NeuroBridge-S4 is a stack of layers, each adding interpretive value. The table below makes that value explicit: raw variables are hard to read; each subsequent layer adds structure until the output is an actionable monitoring priority.

Technical cell: builds the layer-value table and figure.

In [26]:

18. Individual Adaptation Profile Reports¶

The final per-member output is a human-readable report, not just a chart. Each report lists the top deviating features, the most affected biological domains, the BACI score/category and its sensitivity note, a short network interpretation, and monitoring priorities, follow-up data streams, and countermeasure considerations - all framed as decision-support. No diagnosis, no treatment. Reports are saved to results/adaptation_profiles.txt.

Technical cell: generates one adaptation profile report per pseudo-crew member.

In [27]:
# --- Generate one adaptation profile report per pseudo-crew member -------
DOMAIN_FOLLOWUP = {
    "Cardiovascular regulation": "HRV / autonomic monitoring; resting HR and blood-pressure tracking",
    "Metabolic regulation": "fasting glucose and lipid re-check; nutrition / metabolic follow-up",
    "Body composition / physical status": "body-composition tracking; physical conditioning load review",
    "Inflammation / immune-adjacent": "immune biomarker follow-up (CRP, white-cell differential); stress-immune panel",
    "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying": "hemoglobin / hematocrit follow-up; oxygen-carrying capacity",
    "Recovery-related markers": "albumin / creatinine recovery markers; recovery-trajectory tracking",
}
DOMAIN_PATTERN = {
    "Cardiovascular regulation": "Autonomic / cardiovascular strain",
    "Metabolic regulation": "Metabolic / fatigue pattern",
    "Body composition / physical status": "Physical-status shift",
    "Inflammation / immune-adjacent": "Stress-immune coupling",
    "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying": "Oxygen-carrying shift",
    "Recovery-related markers": "Delayed recovery pattern",
}
DOMAIN_COUNTERMEASURE = {
    "Cardiovascular regulation": "autonomic/cardiovascular monitoring consideration",
    "Metabolic regulation": "nutrition / metabolic review consideration",
    "Body composition / physical status": "physical-conditioning load consideration",
    "Inflammation / immune-adjacent": "immune follow-up and recovery-tracking consideration",
    "Hematologic / oxygen-carrying": "oxygen-carrying capacity monitoring consideration",
    "Recovery-related markers": "recovery-protocol and hydration/nutrition consideration",
}
BACI_INTERPRETATION = {
    "low coherence": "Deviations look isolated; no coordinated multi-system adaptation signal at this time.",
    "mild coherence": "A modest, partly coordinated signal; routine monitoring is reasonable.",
    "moderate coherence": "Several systems shift together; this warrants prioritized monitoring.",
    "high coherence": "A strongly coordinated multi-system signal; highest monitoring priority among the crew.",
}


def build_report(member_label):
    seqn = int(member_label.split()[1])
    lines = []
    add = lines.append
    add("=" * 74)
    add("NeuroBridge-S4  |  Individual Adaptation Profile")
    add(f"Pseudo-crew participant (anonymized NHANES SEQN): {seqn}")
    add("Data source: real NHANES 2017-2018 public data (NOT Artemis II astronaut data)")
    add("=" * 74)

    z_row = deviation_scores.loc[member_label].dropna()
    top_feats = z_row.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5)
    add("")
    add("Top deviating features (vs health-filtered reference cohort):")
    for label, _ in top_feats.items():
        add(f"   - {label:38s} reference deviation z = {z_row[label]:+.2f}")

    dom_row = domain_scores.loc[member_label].dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)
    add("")
    add("Top affected biological domains:")
    for d, v in dom_row.head(3).items():
        add(f"   - {d:42s} mean |z| = {v:.2f}")

    score = baci_scores.loc[member_label, "BACI"]
    cat = baci_scores.loc[member_label, "category"]
    add("")
    add(f"BACI score (signal-triage, not a diagnosis): {score:.0f} / 100  ({cat})")
    add(f"   {BACI_INTERPRETATION[cat]}")
    add(f"   BACI sensitivity: crew ranking across thresholds 0.75/1.00/1.25 was "
        f"{'stable' if ranking_stable else 'threshold-sensitive (review borderline members)'}.")

    add("")
    add("Network / graph interpretation summary:")
    if len(dom_row):
        top_d = dom_row.index[0]
        connected = [b if a == top_d else a for a, b in DOMAIN_EDGES if top_d in (a, b)]
        add(f"   - Primary cluster: {top_d}")
        if connected:
            add(f"   - Biologically linked systems to watch alongside it: {', '.join(connected)}")
        add(f"   - Pattern label: {DOMAIN_PATTERN.get(top_d, 'mixed pattern')}")

    add("")
    add("Monitoring priorities (decision-support, not treatment):")
    for d, _ in dom_row.head(3).items():
        add(f"   - {DOMAIN_FOLLOWUP.get(d, 'targeted follow-up sampling')}")

    add("")
    add("Follow-up data streams to prioritize:")
    for s in ["sleep / circadian monitoring", "HRV / autonomic monitoring", "immune biomarker follow-up",
              "metabolic follow-up", "cognitive performance monitoring", "validated psychological self-report",
              "recovery-trajectory tracking"]:
        add(f"   - {s}")

    add("")
    add("Countermeasure considerations (categories only, not prescriptions):")
    for d, _ in dom_row.head(2).items():
        add(f"   - {DOMAIN_COUNTERMEASURE.get(d, 'targeted monitoring consideration')}")

    add("")
    add("Note: This is decision-support only. No medical diagnosis. No treatment recommendation.")
    add("")
    return "\n".join(lines)


reports = [build_report(label) for label in domain_scores.index]
full_report_text = "\n".join(reports)
report_path = RESULTS / "adaptation_profiles.txt"
report_path.write_text(full_report_text)
print(f"Wrote {len(reports)} adaptation profiles -> {report_path}\n")
print(reports[0] if reports else "No reports generated (structure-only fallback).")

19. Artemis II Translation Map¶

NeuroBridge-S4 is designed specifically for the three Artemis II human research study streams, not as a generic wellness model. Each stream maps to a NeuroBridge-S4 layer with clear HRP value:

Artemis II stream Data type NeuroBridge-S4 layer HRP value
Standard Measures Biomarkers, physiological/functional state Reference deviation + biological domains Which systems deviate, and how unusually
ARCHeR Sleep, activity, well-being, social interaction Behavioral signals -> autonomic/cognitive interpretation Sleep/circadian and workload context
Immune Biomarkers Stress-immune markers Inflammation/immune domain + stress-immune coherence Stress-immune coupling and follow-up priorities

Important scope note. In actual Artemis II use, NHANES would not be the main target - it would be one lower-level reference layer. The real value would come from combining: an individual pre-mission baseline, in-mission measurements, post-mission recovery data, actigraphy/sleep, immune/stress biomarkers, cognitive performance, and validated psychological self-report.

def flow_box(x, y, w, h, text, color):
    box = FancyBboxPatch((x, y), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.08",
                         linewidth=1.5, edgecolor="#333333", facecolor=color)

    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x1, y1), (x2, y2), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=18,
                                 linewidth=1.6, color="#444444"))

20. Acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability layer (conceptual)¶

Acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability is treated as a monitoring context, not a diagnosis. States such as derealization-like detachment, sensory unreality, or emotional numbing should not be inferred from biomarkers, and this framework does not attempt to detect or diagnose them.

Instead, NeuroBridge-S4 can flag convergence among sleep disruption, autonomic strain, stress biology, immune/inflammatory shift, cognitive fatigue, and validated self-report as a reason to prioritize cognitive and psychological monitoring - especially under the combined pressure of mission stress and isolation. The terms used are deliberately careful: acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability, cognitive-perceptual strain, emotional regulation load, evidence-based psychological indicators, validated self-report, and monitoring priority.

Technical cell: conceptual vulnerability graph (a monitoring flag, not a diagnosis).

In [29]:
# --- Figure: acute cognitive-perceptual vulnerability layer --------------
Ga = nx.DiGraph()
contributors = [
    "Sleep\ndisruption", "Autonomic\nstrain", "Stress\nbiology",
    "Immune /\ninflammatory shift", "Cognitive\nfatigue", "Validated\nself-report",
]
center = "Acute cognitive-\nperceptual vulnerability\n(monitoring flag)"
for c in contributors:
    Ga.add_edge(c, center)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 8))
posa = nx.spring_layout(Ga, seed=RANDOM_SEED, k=1.4, iterations=250)
node_colors = ["#fbb4ae" if n == center else "#b3cde3" for n in Ga.nodes()]
node_sizes = [4200 if n == center else 2600 for n in Ga.nodes()]
nx.draw_networkx_edges(Ga, posa, ax=ax, edge_color="#888888", width=1.6,
                       arrowstyle="-|>", arrowsize=18, min_target_margin=24)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(Ga, posa, ax=ax, node_color=node_colors, node_size=node_sizes,
                       edgecolors="#333333", linewidths=1.4)
nx.draw_networkx_labels(Ga, posa, ax=ax, font_size=8.5)
ax.set_title("When should HRP prioritize cognitive/psychological monitoring?\nConceptual monitoring flag from convergent conditions - NOT a diagnosis")
ax.axis("off")

21. Crew-Level Summary¶

For Artemis II, a crew-level summary must not average away individual differences. Instead it surfaces each member's top system, coherence, primary pattern, and the monitoring priority and follow-up data stream that follow.

Technical cell: builds the crew-level summary table, CSV, and figure.

In [30]:

22. What HRP could do with this output¶

These are illustrative monitoring considerations, not treatment guidance.

  • If the output shows sleep/circadian + autonomic + fatigue coherence -> HRP may prioritize sleep/circadian monitoring, HRV/autonomic monitoring, cognitive performance tracking, and workload-pacing consideration.
  • If the output shows stress-immune coherence -> HRP may prioritize immune biomarker follow-up, stress-load monitoring, and recovery tracking.
  • If the output shows an isolated biomarker deviation -> HRP may treat it as a lower-confidence finding requiring confirmation before action.
  • If the output shows a delayed-recovery pattern -> HRP may prioritize post-mission recovery follow-up.

In every case, the output answers "what should HRP look at more closely?" - never "what treatment should be given?"

24. Conclusion¶

This notebook demonstrates the core logic of NeuroBridge-S4 using real public proxy data. It shows how to build a health-filtered terrestrial reference approximation, select a real n = 4 pseudo-crew of real participants, normalize individual measurements against that reference space, group changes into biological domains, compute a transparent Biological Adaptation Coherence Index (BACI) with a sensitivity check, separate three distinct graph types (conceptual, observed, decision-support), and generate adaptation management profiles. The framework supports astronaut physical and psychological state management by connecting biochemical, physiological, cognitive, and evidence-based psychological signals into operationally meaningful monitoring priorities.
